what: LandBridge owns land in the Permian Basin. It does not drill wells; it owns the surface rights over about 270,000 acres and charges oil companies for using that surface — for well pads, roads, pipelines, electricity lines, water disposal, sand mining and, increasingly, data centres.
customers: Oil and gas producers operating in the Permian Basin who need surface access, water handling and infrastructure corridors, plus industrial and data centre developers seeking large sites with power.
money: Payments for well pads, roads, pipelines and infrastructure on its land.
Brackish water sales, sand and other materials extracted from the land.
Oil and gas royalties and other
Mineral royalties and emerging revenue from data centre and industrial development.
moat: Surface land above the most productive oil basin in the world is a finite asset with no operating costs: LandBridge collects payments for activity on its land without paying for wells, equipment or labour. Because its acreage is contiguous and large, it can host pipelines and infrastructure corridors that need a continuous route, which fragmented ownership cannot offer.
risks: The shares trade at about 54.5 times earnings, 36.2 times EV/EBITDA and 22.4 times sales — an extremely high price on $245.5M of revenue.
Revenue depends entirely on activity levels in the Permian Basin, which follow the oil price.
Debt of $570.7M against $30.7M of cash is meaningful for a company with revenue of this size.
The company listed recently, so there is no record of how the revenue behaves through a downturn in drilling.
Seven analysts average an $89.57 target, about 25% above the current price, on a very high starting multiple.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $72.9M in 2023 to $199.1M in 2025, with trailing revenue of $245.5M.
A net margin of 15.1% understates the economics: free cash flow of $166.5M on $245.5M of revenue is a 68% conversion, because the land requires almost no spending.
Surface rights above the most active oil basin in the world are a finite asset that cannot be created.
Data centre development on its land is a genuinely new revenue source, driven by the combination of space, power access and gas supply.
Water handling and disposal revenue grows with drilling activity but is contracted rather than commodity-priced.
watch: Surface use agreements signed and the data centre pipeline. The land is fixed; what changes is how many ways it is being monetised, and new agreements are the forward indicator.
view: LandBridge is an unusual and rather elegant idea: own the ground above the busiest oil basin in the world and charge everybody who needs to use it. Oil companies need well pads, roads, pipeline corridors, electricity lines, water disposal and sand. LandBridge provides the surface and collects payments without drilling a well, buying a rig or employing a crew. Free cash flow of $167 million on $246 million of revenue — a 68% conversion — is what that absence of operating costs looks like.

The contiguity of the acreage is a detail worth dwelling on, because it is the real competitive advantage. A pipeline needs a continuous route, and negotiating with fifty separate landowners is slow, expensive and sometimes impossible. A single owner of a large contiguous block can offer a corridor immediately. That is why LandBridge’s land is worth more per acre than the same acreage split among many owners, and it is not something a competitor can assemble now.

The newest and most interesting revenue source is data centres. The combination LandBridge offers — large flat sites, access to electricity, and natural gas available on the spot for generation — is exactly what AI computing needs and what is scarce everywhere else. That revenue is early and the contracts are few, but it is genuinely additive and has nothing to do with the oil price.

What I cannot get comfortable with is the price. At 54.5 times earnings, 36.2 times EV/EBITDA and 22.4 times sales, the market is valuing $246 million of revenue at $5.5 billion, which requires both continued Permian activity and the data centre business becoming large. The company listed recently and has never experienced a drilling downturn, so nobody knows how much of this revenue is resilient and how much simply stops when rig counts fall. The business model is excellent; the multiple assumes nothing goes wrong and several new things go right.
bull: Permian activity stays strong while data centre and industrial development opens a second revenue stream on the same land, at 68% cash conversion and no operating cost.
bear: The oil price falls, Permian drilling slows, and a company earning $246 million of revenue at 36 times EV/EBITDA discovers how cyclical its tenants are.
